active.title: Hike the Okutama trail west of Tokyo
active.description: One hour west of Shinjuku by train, Okutama's gorge trails are serious hiking through cedar forest with rope bridges and river crossings — Tokyo day-trippers almost never make it this far.
active.bonus: Cross the gorge suspension bridge. Look down. Keep going.

active.title: Cycle from Asakusa to Odaiba via the waterfront
active.description: The 20km waterfront cycling route from Asakusa to Odaiba via Tsukishima passes through industrial ports, fish markets, and a giant Gundam statue with no traffic to worry about.
active.bonus: Get to Odaiba before 9am. The bay is silent that early.

active.title: Sunrise yoga at Shinjuku Gyoen
active.description: The garden opens at 9am but the outer paths are accessible at first light — a sunrise yoga session in the Japanese garden before the day starts is one of Tokyo's great secrets.
active.bonus: Get there before the gate opens. The 15 minutes outside the wall are the best.

active.title: Morning run around the Imperial Palace gardens
active.description: The 5km outer loop of the Imperial Palace is Tokyo's most iconic running route — hundreds of runners go clockwise every morning in a silent, highly organized flow.
active.bonus: Go counter-clockwise. You'll notice every face.

active.title: Kendo Class at Kodokan Budokan
active.description: Step onto the polished floor of the Kodokan — the global home of judo — and take a beginner's session in a martial art practiced here since 1882.
active.bonus: Bow correctly every single time you enter and exit the mat — don't let a sensei have to remind you twice.

active.title: Bouldering at B-PUMP Ogikubo
active.description: Tokyo's climbing culture is fierce and technical — B-PUMP draws serious locals to one of the city's best bouldering walls, where the problem-setting is world class.
active.bonus: Ask the strongest person in the room to set you a project route — attempt it until your forearms give out.

active.title: Cycle the Tamagawa Cycling Road
active.description: Rent a road bike and follow the Tama River 20km from Futako-Tamagawa to the coast — Tokyo peels away and becomes something genuinely wild.
active.bonus: Ride all the way to Tokyo Bay, touch the water, then turn back — no shortcuts.

active.title: Dawn Run Along the Imperial Palace Outer Gardens
active.description: Tokyo's power runners circle the 5km Imperial Palace loop at sunrise — join them and feel the city's quiet ambition before the trains fill.
active.bonus: Run the full loop twice without stopping — nod to every runner you pass.

active.title: Bouldering at Crux in Nakameguro
active.description: A multi-level bouldering gym in a converted Nakameguro warehouse with a serious local climbing community — day passes include shoe rental and the route setters update problems on a regular rotation.
active.bonus: Ask a regular to show you their favourite problem on the current set. Match it, then find one on your own.

active.title: Imperial Palace Morning Run
active.description: The 5km loop around the moat and outer gardens of the Imperial Palace is Tokyo's unofficial morning running club — from 5:30am, hundreds of runners in all conditions share one of the flattest and most scenic circuits in the city.
active.bonus: Run the full 5km without stopping. Then do one more kilometre.

active.title: Sumo Morning Practice at Arashio Stable
active.description: Arashio is the only sumo stable in Tokyo that lets the public observe morning keiko (practice) through a street-facing window — arrive by 7:30am, stand in silence, and watch 300-pound athletes move with unsettling speed.
active.bonus: Stay for the full session. Don't leave before practice ends. A small bow as you leave is appropriate.

foodie.title: Yakitori under the Yurakucho train tracks
foodie.description: The brick arches under the Yamanote Line at Yurakucho have been yakitori stalls since the 1940s — order tsukune, negima, and skin while trains rumble overhead.
foodie.bonus: Order the whole progression: liver, heart, skin, thigh, wing. In that order.

foodie.title: Tsukiji outer market breakfast: tamagoyaki and tuna nigiri
foodie.description: The outer market still operates with vendors slicing, grilling, and serving at 6am — eat as many pieces of fatty tuna as the day allows.
foodie.bonus: Arrive before 7am. The best cuts go fast.

foodie.title: Omakase at Kyubey, Ginza
foodie.description: Surrender the meal entirely to the itamae — no menu, no preferences, no timeline — just 20 courses of whatever arrived from the sea this morning.
foodie.bonus: Tell the chef it's your first omakase. They'll feed you differently.

foodie.title: Tonkatsu at Tonki, Meguro
foodie.description: Asakusa's oldest tonkatsu shops have been frying pork cutlet in the same oil, with the same recipe, since before WWII — eat the katsu curry and understand what institution means.
foodie.bonus: Order without looking at the menu. Just say katsu curry.

foodie.title: Kaiseki at Kagurazaka Ishikawa
foodie.description: A full kaiseki progression through the seasons in a private tatami room — the most considered meal in Japanese food culture — reserve six weeks ahead and dress appropriately.
foodie.bonus: Identify which course represents which season. Ask the server.

foodie.title: Morning mochi at Yanaka Matsunoya
foodie.description: Yanaka's old shitamachi district has traditional wagashi shops making mochi fresh each morning — arrive early, buy three kinds, and eat them on the cemetery steps.
foodie.bonus: Buy the daifuku with red bean. It's non-negotiable.

foodie.title: Tempura at Tsunahachi, Shinjuku
foodie.description: A great tempura counter serves each piece directly from the oil to your plate in sequence — eat immediately, one piece at a time, and don't drown it in sauce.
foodie.bonus: Ask for the kakiage (mixed vegetable fritter) as your last piece.

foodie.title: Ramen counter in Shinjuku's Omoide Yokocho
foodie.description: Memory Lane's tiny yakitori and ramen counters seat six people and have been there since 1945 — squeeze in, order the tonkotsu, and let the smoke do the rest.
foodie.bonus: Sit at the counter. Don't ask for a table. There isn't one.

foodie.title: Depachika Deep Dive at Isetan Shinjuku B2
foodie.description: The basement food hall of Isetan Shinjuku is Tokyo's most dazzling cathedral of food — every artisan confection, pickled thing, and lacquered bento has earned its place.
foodie.bonus: Spend exactly ¥1,000 and make it count — one item, best possible choice, no hesitation.

foodie.title: Tonkatsu Lunch at Maisen, Omotesando
foodie.description: A converted bathhouse in Omotesando serves Tokyo's most iconic tonkatsu — the kurobuta pork is impossibly tender inside a shard-crisp panko shell.
foodie.bonus: Grind your own sesame seeds in the stone mortar at the table before mixing your sauce — don't let anyone help you.

foodie.title: Omakase Sushi at Sushi Saito
foodie.description: One of the hardest reservations on earth delivers nigiri so precise and seasonal it feels less like dinner and more like a private audience with perfection.
foodie.bonus: Ask Saito-san which piece he is most proud of today — then eat it last.

foodie.title: Ramen at Fuunji, Shinjuku
foodie.description: Fuunji's tsukemen — thick noodles dragged through an intensely rich, chicken-based dipping broth — is the kind of bowl that ruins all other ramen for you.
foodie.bonus: Order the largest portion (tokumori) and finish every drop of broth — ask for the hot dashi to thin it at the end, like a regular.

foodie.title: Isetan Shinjuku Depachika Crawl
foodie.description: The basement food halls of Isetan Shinjuku's B1 and B2 floors contain more precision-crafted food per square metre than anywhere on earth — every pastry, bento, wagashi, and prepared dish is worthy of the price tag.
foodie.bonus: Buy one thing from each floor. Eat them in order starting from the sweetest.

foodie.title: Tsukemen at Fuunji in Shinjuku
foodie.description: A 12-seat shop near Shinjuku that's earned a cult reputation for its thick pork-and-fish dipping broth — arrive when it opens or expect a 45-minute queue, and order the regular size your first time.
foodie.bonus: Don't add anything to the dipping broth. Eat it exactly as it arrives.

foodie.title: Solo Ramen at Ichiran
foodie.description: Ichiran's individual booths with a wooden privacy screen, a curtained hatch, and a flavour questionnaire let you design your exact bowl — the perfect ramen experience for one person in a city that rewards solitude.
foodie.bonus: No phone during the meal. Curtain down, screen up, full presence.

foodie.title: Omakase at a Ginza Sushi Counter
foodie.description: Hand yourself over to a Ginza sushi master for 90 minutes — no menu, twelve courses of nigiri pressed in front of you, the chef reading what you need between pieces.
foodie.bonus: Don't use soy sauce on the last three pieces — trust the chef to have seasoned them already.

foodie.title: Yakitori and Highballs Under the Yurakucho Tracks
foodie.description: The brick arches beneath the Yamanote Line at Yurakucho are home to six decades of yakitori stalls — order skewers, add a whisky highball, and sit under the tracks as the trains shake the ceiling every 90 seconds.
foodie.bonus: Stay for at least one full round of drinks after you finish eating. The best conversations happen after the food.

foodie.title: Tsukiji Outer Market Breakfast
foodie.description: The market that fed Tokyo for 80 years still operates in the outer ring — arrive at 7am for tamagoyaki still on the grill, a cup of dashi broth, and the freshest tuna you'll ever eat standing up.
foodie.bonus: Buy something from the fishmongers before you eat — even if it's just dried dashi. Talk to the vendors.

social.title: Cosplay-spotting in Harajuku's Takeshita Street
social.description: Takeshita-dori on a weekend is one of the most visually dense 350 meters in any city — crepes, vintage, Lolita fashion, and teenagers who committed entirely.
social.bonus: Count 10 genuinely great outfits and photograph none of them.

social.title: Golden Gai bar crawl: four bars in one night
social.description: Six alleys, 200 bars, each seating eight to ten people — find ones with no cover charge, order whatever the master is drinking, and stay only until the conversation runs out.
social.bonus: Find a bar with no sign in English. Go in anyway.

social.title: Craft beer at Yanaka Beer Hall
social.description: Yanaka Brewery and a handful of similar operations have brought serious craft beer into Tokyo's most traditional neighbourhood — drink on the street outside if the weather allows.
social.bonus: Try the seasonal. That's why they made it.

social.title: Purikura photo booth session in Akihabara
social.description: Japan's photo booths are six-step productions with lighting rigs, makeup filters, and decoration tools — the results are art-directed nonsense and you'll keep them forever.
social.bonus: Use every decoration tool available. Go fully committed.

social.title: Night at Womb Club, Shibuya
social.description: Club Asia, Womb, or Contact — Tokyo's electronic music scene is technically excellent and the crowds are engaged in a way that disappears before midnight in most cities.
social.bonus: Stay until the trains restart at 5am. Take the first one home.

social.title: Jazz at DUG Bar, Shinjuku
social.description: Tokyo's kissa jazz cafés — where you listen in silence on high-end speakers while the master plays vinyl — are a specific and vanishing institution worth visiting twice.
social.bonus: Don't talk. Listen like you paid for every note.

social.title: Jazz Night at Shinjuku Pit Inn
social.description: Open since 1965, Pit Inn is Tokyo's most serious jazz room — a basement box where world-class musicians play two feet from your face.
social.bonus: Talk to the person next to you between sets — ask them their favorite record and actually listen.

social.title: Sumo Morning Practice at Tomozuna Stable
social.description: Watch elite rikishi train in total silence at a real sumo stable in Ryogoku — an hour of controlled violence and ritual that no museum can replicate.
social.bonus: Bow respectfully at the entrance, stay completely silent, and make eye contact with a wrestler — hold it without flinching.

social.title: Bar Hop Through Golden Gai, Shinjuku
social.description: Six narrow alleys packed with 200 six-seat bars — each one a different world, a different owner, a different reason to stay for one more drink.
social.bonus: Walk in alone to a bar where you're the only foreigner and start a conversation without using your phone as a crutch.

social.title: Karaoke Private Box at Shidax, Shibuya
social.description: Book a private room at Shidax, order unlimited drinks, and discover which song you were actually born to perform.
social.bonus: Sing one song in a language you don't speak — full commitment, no laughing until it's over.

social.title: Kaiseki Dinner at Kikunoi Akasaka
social.description: The Tokyo branch of Kyoto's most celebrated kaiseki house runs an eight-course seasonal menu through which the chef encodes the current month — cherry blossoms in the broth, autumn leaves in the plating, winter in the texture of every dish.
social.bonus: Order the sake pairing and drink every course in the order it arrives. Don't question the sequence.

social.title: Karaoke Private Room in Shinjuku
social.description: Book a private booth at Big Echo or Karaoke Kan for two hours — the rooms soundproof everything, the tambourines are real, drinks come through a hatch, and it's impossible to have a bad time in a group of more than two.
social.bonus: One song each. No skipping. Everyone sings the whole thing.

social.title: Golden Gai Bar Crawl
social.description: Shinjuku's infamous alley cluster holds 200 bars spread across six lanes — most seat between four and eight people, every one has a theme, and you're expected to move on after two drinks.
social.bonus: Visit at least four bars. Start a real conversation in three of them.

social.title: Omoide Yokocho Memory Lane
social.description: A narrow alley of post-war izakayas in West Shinjuku that have barely changed since 1946 — yakitori smoke, salarymen, and enough whisky highballs that the distinctions between strangers start to dissolve.
social.bonus: Sit at a shared counter. Talk to whoever is next to you, even if they don't speak English.

adventure.title: Midnight cycling from Shibuya to Odaiba bridge
adventure.description: Tokyo at midnight by bike is a different city — empty roads, lit bridges, Rainbow Bridge glowing over the bay, and the whole thing yours for the cost of a rental.
adventure.bonus: Cross Rainbow Bridge on foot from the bike path. The bay view is the payoff.

adventure.title: Climb Tokyo Skytree and spot a neighbourhood from 634m
adventure.description: The world's second-tallest tower gives a 634-meter view over 38 million people — take the top deck, pick a neighbourhood you've been to, and try to find it in the sprawl.
adventure.bonus: Find Shinjuku, Shibuya, and Asakusa from the top. All three.

adventure.title: SCRAP Real Escape Game, Akihabara
adventure.description: Several Akihabara escape rooms run Japanese-only scenarios — the puzzle logic is universal even when the text isn't, and the panic is the same in any language.
adventure.bonus: No translation app. Solve it with what you have.

adventure.title: Mount Fuji day trip: Fuji Five Lakes trail
adventure.description: Two hours west of Tokyo by bus, Fuji's trails range from lakeside walks to the crater climb — pick a trail above 2,000m and earn the view of the city you came from.
adventure.bonus: Start before sunrise. The mountain is clearest before clouds build.

adventure.title: Tokyo Drift at Odaiba Go-Kart
adventure.description: Strap into a street-legal go-kart dressed as your favorite character and blast through Odaiba's waterfront streets with Rainbow Bridge as your backdrop.
adventure.bonus: Pick the most embarrassing costume available — bonus spark if it's a vegetable.

adventure.title: Roof Scramble at Takao-san via Inariyama Trail
adventure.description: Tokyo's most beloved mountain delivers a ridge-line forest trail, tengu statues, and a skyline payoff that makes you forget the city exists.
adventure.bonus: Ask a stranger at the summit to point out Mount Fuji — then buy them a cup of amazake from the stall.

adventure.title: Night Kayak on the Sumida River
adventure.description: Paddle past illuminated bridges and the Asahi Flame Building on a guided night kayak through old Edo's main waterway.
adventure.bonus: Dip your hand in the Sumida and make a wish — then look up the river's transformation from open sewer to this.

adventure.title: Scramble at Shibuya Crossing
adventure.description: Stand at the center of the world's busiest intersection and let 3,000 people swirl around you like a human tide.
adventure.bonus: Stop dead center when the light changes and hold perfectly still while the crowd parts around you.

adventure.title: Day Trip to Nikko by Train
adventure.description: The Tosho-gu shrine complex in Nikko is one of Japan's most elaborately carved sacred sites — gold leaf, cedar avenues, and the three wise monkeys original, two hours from Shinjuku on the Tobu Nikko Line.
adventure.bonus: Find the sleeping cat carving (Nemuri-neko) above the inner shrine gates — it's small and most people walk past it.

adventure.title: Cycle Through Yanaka Old Town
adventure.description: Yanaka is what Tokyo looked like before the earthquakes and the bombs — narrow lanes, wooden shopfronts, and a cemetery full of Edo-period graves that locals use as a park on weekday mornings.
adventure.bonus: Lock the bike at the cemetery entrance and walk the rest. Yanaka moves at foot pace.

adventure.title: Shimokitazawa Record Shops and Vintage Stores
adventure.description: The neighbourhood that resisted Tokyo's development is a maze of vinyl shops, indie theater marquees, and thrift stores crammed into alleys too narrow for cars — best explored on foot with no plan.
adventure.bonus: Buy one record you've never heard. Play it that night.

chill.title: Afternoon in the covered arcades of Koenji
chill.description: Koenji's roofed shotengai shopping streets hold vintage clothing, used bookshops, cafés, and small live music venues in a neighbourhood that hasn't been gentrified yet.
chill.bonus: Walk every covered arcade. Don't cut back. Walk them all.

chill.title: Vinyl hunting at Disk Union Shimokitazawa
chill.description: Shimokitazawa has the best concentration of vinyl shops in Asia — find one that specializes in a genre you half-know and let an afternoon disappear in the stacks.
chill.bonus: Buy one record you've never heard. Take it home and play it first.

chill.title: Early morning at Senso-ji temple before the crowds
chill.description: Senso-ji at dawn — incense, monks, and the Kaminarimon gate in morning light before any tourist has arrived — is the most peaceful you'll feel in Tokyo.
chill.bonus: Arrive before 6:30am. You'll have it almost entirely to yourself.

chill.title: Tea ceremony in a Hamarikyu garden tea house
chill.description: The traditional tea house in Hamarikyu's garden sits in a tidal pond with skyscrapers behind it — a 500-year-old ritual surrounded by the 21st century.
chill.bonus: Move slowly. Follow the host's pace exactly. Don't rush the bowl.

chill.title: Read manga in Nakano Broadway café
chill.description: Nakano Broadway is Tokyo's most obsessive collector's mall — find the manga café inside, rent a cubicle, and read something you can't get in translation.
chill.bonus: Finish an entire volume in the session. Don't stop in the middle.

chill.title: Wander Yanaka cemetery and old shitamachi at dawn
chill.description: Yanaka survived the war and the earthquakes — its cemetery and shopping street at dawn are the old Tokyo that most of the city has already lost.
chill.bonus: Walk through the cemetery, not around it. Take the longest path.

chill.title: Cherry blossoms in Shinjuku Gyoen in spring
chill.description: Shinjuku Gyoen has 1,000 cherry trees and bans alcohol — the result is a calm, beautiful hanami in the middle of the world's largest city that feels nothing like the chaos outside its walls.
chill.bonus: Find the weeping cherry trees in the Japanese garden section. They bloom differently.

chill.title: Sunrise at Senso-ji Before the Crowds
chill.description: Arrive at Asakusa's 1,400-year-old temple at 6am and you get incense smoke, orange lantern light, and almost no one — a version of Tokyo most visitors never see.
chill.bonus: Draw an omikuji fortune slip — if it's bad luck (kyō), tie it to the rack and walk away without looking back.

chill.title: Onsen Soak at Thermae-Yu, Shinjuku
chill.description: A genuine hot-spring bathhouse in the heart of Shinjuku pulls real sodium bicarbonate water from 1,700 meters below — the silk-water feeling is addictive.
chill.bonus: Try the outdoor rotenburo even in winter — stay until your shoulders are completely loose.

chill.title: Golden Hour at Shinjuku Gyoen
chill.description: Tokyo's finest garden spreads 58 acres of French, English, and Japanese landscapes just minutes from Shinjuku's neon chaos — the contrast is the whole point.
chill.bonus: Find the largest plane tree in the French garden and sit with your back against it for ten full, silent minutes.

chill.title: Afternoon Tea at Kagizen Yoshifusa, Gion-style in Yanaka
chill.description: Yanaka's old-town streets hide Kayaba Coffee, a 1938 kissaten where time genuinely stops over egg salad sandwiches and hand-drip coffee.
chill.bonus: Leave your phone in your bag for the entire visit — observe the room instead.

chill.title: teamLab Planets Digital Art Walk
chill.description: Four large-scale rooms you move through barefoot — mirrors, water, light, and projection that surround you on all sides in a way that photographs genuinely cannot capture.
chill.bonus: Enter the water room last and stay until the staff asks you to leave.

chill.title: Shinjuku Gyoen National Garden
chill.description: A 144-acre park of French, English, and Japanese gardens within walking distance of the hyperactivity of Shinjuku — no alcohol, no loud noise, and a greenhouse of subtropical plants that makes you forget the city exists.
chill.bonus: Find a bench away from the paths and sit for 20 uninterrupted minutes. No headphones.

chill.title: Thermae Yu Bathhouse in Shinjuku
chill.description: A modern sento open until midnight seven days a week — alternating mineral baths, jet pools, saunas, and a rest lounge where Tokyo's most wound-up citizens come to stop.
chill.bonus: End your session in the cold bath and stay in for 60 full seconds. Count them.

chill.title: Senso-ji Temple at Dawn
chill.description: Asakusa's 7th-century temple is mobbed by noon and empty at 5:30am — the Nakamise shopping street is shuttered, incense smoke rises in silence, and the Kaminarimon gate looks exactly like the photographs, except you're the only one there.
chill.bonus: Light an incense stick and let the smoke wash over you before entering the main hall. Do it properly.
